# Logic model and evaluation plan

Two of the most commonly requested and most commonly weak sections. A funder
reading a vague evaluation plan assumes the organization will not know whether
its program worked — and neither will they.

## Logic model skeleton

| | |
|---|---|
| **Inputs** | Staff and facilitators, curriculum, court/IDRC referral partnerships, treatment provider relationships, facilities, funding |
| **Activities** | [[PLACEHOLDER: workshops delivered, one-on-one support sessions, referrals made, family sessions]] |
| **Outputs** | [[PLACEHOLDER: # participants, # sessions, # referrals completed, # families served]] |
| **Short-term outcomes** | [[PLACEHOLDER: knowledge gain, treatment engagement, reduced symptom severity]] |
| **Intermediate outcomes** | [[PLACEHOLDER: treatment retention, stable housing, employment, reduced violations]] |
| **Long-term outcomes** | [[PLACEHOLDER: reduced recidivism, sustained recovery, family stability]] |

## Measurement

| Outcome | Instrument | When collected | Who collects |
|---|---|---|---|
| [[PLACEHOLDER]] | [[PLACEHOLDER: pre/post survey, standardized instrument, court records]] | | |

Validated instruments are worth naming if used — reviewers recognize them and
they signal methodological seriousness. If the organization uses informal
pre/post surveys, say so honestly and describe plans to strengthen measurement.

## Honest positioning for a young organization

If longitudinal outcome data does not exist yet, do not manufacture it. Write:
what is currently tracked, what the grant period would let the organization
begin tracking, and the specific plan for doing so. A credible plan to build
measurement beats a fabricated result, and it survives a site visit.
